tasks.file_line: AGENTS.md 'Two products, one repository' rules 1 and 3, sources/TinyTitanLib/*.swift (22 public types, 88 public declarations, 291 package), tools/lint.sh (no facade check)
tasks.title: Nothing enforces the library facade: `public` in `TinyTitanLib` is a promise carried only by the reviewer's memory, and so are 'imports no NIO' and 'keeps stdout clean'
tasks.category: unenforced documented standard (missing gate)
tasks.discovered-by: AUD-151 fix, sibling sweep (asking which other written standards are carried by habit alone)
tasks.evidence-before: AGENTS.md states three properties of `sources/TinyTitanLib/` as rules: every public declaration there is deliberate and 'nothing becomes `public` by accident' (rule 3, with `package` named as the default for everything internal); the library 'imports no NIO' (rule 1); and nothing in it may `print`, because stdout belongs to the embedding program. `tools/lint.sh` has fourteen checks and none of them looks at access level, imports or stdout in that target; swiftlint's config has no such rule either; and `Package.swift` grants `TinyTitanLib` whatever it declares. Measured 2026-10-06, all three properties hold: 22 public types (Engine, Session, EngineConfiguration and its seven vocabulary enums/structs, ChatMessage/Role/Prompt/GenerationOptions/GenerationEvent/GenerationSummary/GenerationStopReason/DecodeStopReason/ToolCall/ToolDefinition, ModelDescriptor, TinyTitanError), 88 public declarations against 291 `package`, no `import NIO*` in the target, and zero `print(` / `FileHandle.standardOutput` occurrences. The finding is not a violation today, it is that the standard has no teeth: adding one `public func` to `ServerModelSession.swift` or one stray `print("loaded")` to the loading path is a permanent API promise or a corrupted consumer stdout, and the compiler, the fourteen gates and the tests all stay silent. That is the same failure mode AUD-151 just closed for file length - a number stated in prose, carried by habit, and quietly out of date within a week - and this one is on the surface an external package depends on, which is what `examples/embedded` exists to prove still builds.
tasks.fix-summary:
One gate, `tools/lint.sh library-facade`, and it is in the `all` chain, so CI runs it without a workflow edit. The row's `evidence-after` asked for the three properties as data; what landed holds them with two mechanisms because they are two kinds of promise. (a) The public surface is a ratchet over `tools/library-facade-baseline.txt`, one row per *declaration* (88 rows, `path:kind:name`), not one per type: the row left that choice to `docs/plan-embedded-library.md` and the owner, and the wider reading costs nothing here while being strictly stronger -- it is what lets the gate see one of `Session.respond`'s two overloads vanish behind its twin's exemption, which a per-type list cannot. Comparison is a multiset (`sort` without `-u`) for exactly that reason. NEW and STALE both fail, so an exemption cannot be reused, and a *missing* allowlist fails rather than blessing the tree -- the deliberate path is `FACADE_UPDATE=1 tools/lint.sh library-facade`, which rewrites the file so the diff is what a reviewer reads. (b) Rule 1 has no baseline and no opt-out because its correct count is zero: `tools/library-facade-rules.py` flags `import …NIO` and any stdout write (`print(`/`printf(`/`puts(`/`FileHandle.standardOutput`/`stdout`), skipping comment lines -- it must, because `ServerLog.swift`'s doc comment states this rule back at itself and a gate that fails on prose is a gate people learn to distrust.

Two scanner properties the first probe found and the code now handles, neither of which the row asked for: `open` is a wider promise than `public` (it also grants overridability outside the module) so it counts as surface, and leading attributes are stripped before the modifier is tested -- a matcher that only looks at what a line starts with would have missed `@discardableResult public func` entirely, which is the same blind spot as the `public`/`package` split it was written to police. Neither form exists in the library today, so the measured surface is unchanged at 88 and the widened matcher found nothing new; it is proved by the mutation, not by a diff.

The row's own numbers are stale and corrected forward: it says `tools/lint.sh` has fourteen checks, and by the time this was worked the script ran fifteen (file-length and test-hollow landed after the row was filed, `unbounded-read` before). `22 public types / 88 declarations / 291 package / zero NIO / zero print` re-measured as exact.

The sibling defect this surfaced is in the documentation of the gate set, and this commit is a live instance of it: `library-facade` made the counts in `RELEASE.md` and `ci.yml`'s step name wrong the moment it landed, which is AUD-160's whole claim. Both now point at `tools/lint.sh`'s usage header instead of carrying a second copy. `AGENTS.md` still says "thirteen checks" and is the maintainer's file -- reported as an owner action, not edited here.
tasks.evidence-after:
Clean tree: `tools/lint.sh library-facade` exits 0 with `ok (88 public declarations, all allowlisted)` and `ok (no NIO import, no stdout write, in 33 files)`.

Sixteen mutation arms, run against the live tree and reverted (full table in `docs/audit-2026-10-06/tool-coverage.md`): 16/16 behaved as required. Ratchet -- (1) a new `public struct` fails with `NEW:`; (2) renaming `Engine.swift`'s `prefillChunk` while its row stays fails with `STALE:`; (3) deleting one of the two identical `:func:respond` rows fails as `NEW:`, which is the multiset property; (4) deleting a unique row fails as `NEW:`; (5) moving the allowlist away fails with `no allowlist at tools/library-facade-baseline.txt`, never a silent bless; (9) `FACADE_UPDATE=1` on a row-missing tree exits 0 with `allowlist rewritten` and puts the row back. Matcher -- (6) `@discardableResult public func` fails and names `audit158Attr` (the line-start matcher would have skipped it); (7) a bare unnameable `public` fails with `UNRESOLVED:` plus file and line; (8) `open class` fails as new surface. Rule 1 -- (10) `import NIOCore` fails with `NIO sources/TinyTitanLib/Engine.swift:2`; (11) a `public func` whose body is `print("mutant")` fails with `STDOUT`; (12) the word `stdout` in a doc comment exits 0. Refusal-to-pass-vacuously -- (13) `ROOT` at a directory whose `sources/TinyTitanLib/` holds no Swift exits 1 `cannot scan …: no Swift files`; (14) a nonexistent `ROOT` exits 1 `cannot scan …: not a directory`. Revert -- (15) `git status` byte-identical to before the probe, and (16) the gate green again.

Other gates re-run on the committed tree: `tools/lint.sh shell` exit 0 (27 scripts, system bash 3.2.57), `tools/lint.sh shellcheck` exit 0 (0.11.0, 27 scripts, no warnings), `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH tools/lint.sh python` exit 0 (ruff 0.16.7, check and format clean, parses under 3.13), `ruby -ryaml` on `ci.yml` parses. No Swift source changed, so the suite and the golden baseline were **not** re-run for this row -- the gate is tooling-only, and that is the honest scope rather than a claim of a full green. `tools/lint.sh python` on the default PATH exits 1 here for an unrelated pre-existing reason: Homebrew's ruff 0.16.10 in `/opt/homebrew/bin` shadows the pinned pipx 0.16.7 in `~/.local/bin`. That is a PATH-order fact about this host, not a missing pin, and the gate's failure message names exactly that.

tasks.file_line: RELEASE.md:26-31 (rule 2), tools/release.sh:47-48,310,369-377, tools/build_library.sh:97
tasks.title: RELEASE.md requires `lipo -archs <binary>` to report exactly `arm64` and nothing in the release path ever runs lipo; the only arm64 claim in a shipped artifact is its filename
tasks.category: unenforced documented standard (missing gate)
tasks.discovered-by: AUD-151 fix, sibling sweep (asking which other written standards are carried by habit alone)
tasks.evidence-before: RELEASE.md rule 2 is stated twice, in the non-negotiables of AGENTS.md and in full in the release standard: 'Build native `arm64` ... Never `--arch x86_64`, never `ARCHS=arm64 x86_64`, and never `lipo -create`' and '**Assert it** - `lipo -archs <binary>` must report exactly `arm64`. A build that silently produced a fat binary is a release defect, not a build option.' `grep -rn lipo tools/` returns **nothing**: the word appears in this repository's tooling only inside a comment in .github/workflows/codeql.yml:89. What the release path does check is names, not bytes - `tools/release.sh:47-48` builds the stage and archive paths as `tinytitan-$VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz`, :310 copies resource bundles, :369-377 asserts the library archive carries `libTinyTitanLib.a`, `libTinyTitanLib.dylib`, the module and the Metal bundle by *member name* (`tar tzf | grep -q`), and `tools/build_library.sh:97` asserts the dylib's install name with `otool -D`. An x86_64-only or fat Mach-O staged under those names would pass every one of them: the arch is asserted nowhere in `tools/release.sh`, nowhere in `tools/build_library.sh`, and nowhere in CI (which builds and tests, and does not stage a release artifact). Measured on the current tree, the claim happens to hold - `lipo -archs` on `.build/release/TinyTitanCLI`, `.build/release/TinyTitanServer` and `.build/release/libTinyTitanLib.a` each report exactly `arm64` - which is the point: the promise is currently true because of how SwiftPM was invoked, and nothing would notice the day it is not. The consequence of a miss is not cosmetic: the artifact is downloaded by name as 'prebuilt binaries (macOS, Apple Silicon / arm64)' (release.sh:316), Rosetta would hide an x86_64 slice on this host, and the sha256 published in the release notes would certify the wrong bytes for the platform the release exists to serve.
tasks.fix-summary: The assertion now runs inside the release path, in one implementation with three call sites. `tools/assert-arch.sh` (new, 98 lines) is sourced, not copied: it is a library of `assert_arm64_dir` / `assert_arm64_archive` and, when invoked directly, a CLI that dispatches on file shape (single file by magic, directory, archive). Detection is by first-four-bytes magic against the full Mach-O set - thin 32/64 in either byte order, fat 32/64, and `!<arch>` - chosen after measuring that `lipo -archs` on a `.swiftmodule` exits 1 with `cannot mmap() ... errno=22`, so a name- or extension-based scan would have made the gate's own module its first false positive, while a `.a` *is* readable and is therefore in scope rather than a hole. Each candidate must report exactly `arm64`; the two failure messages are distinct by design ('reports arches ...' vs 'lipo cannot read ...'). Call sites: `release.sh` asserts the unpacked engine archive and the unpacked library archive, each **before** that archive's `shasum`, so no checksum is ever taken over unasserted bytes; `build_library.sh` asserts its staging directory, which is the standalone operator path that never goes through `release.sh`; CI asserts the four built products (new step, 'The arm64 promise (RELEASE.md rule 2)'). A stage containing no Mach-O dies rather than passing vacuously. Docs: RELEASE.md §1.2.2 records why the check must be executed rather than recited, part 2's Artifacts bullet names the script and the three places it runs, and `docs/release-process.md` step 4/5 describe the order the checks now run in.
tasks.evidence-after:
Proven by mutation, not by a green run. `docs/audit-2026-10-06/AUD-159-arch-probe.sh` (new, committed) extracts `release.sh`'s own stage -> package -> checksum lines (74 lines) and runs them unmodified: with the real products it asserts then checksums; with `/usr/bin/lipo` (fat) planted as TinyTitanCLI it dies and **no .sha256 exists**; restoring the real binary passes again. The sibling arm does the same for the missing membership loop: without it a three-binary archive gets a checksum, with it TinyTitanBench is named and the checksum refused. Arming the gate directly: engine archive 4 Mach-O each exactly arm64, library archive 2 (its 29 .swiftmodule bitcode files are skipped, as measured), then fat -> "reports arches 'x86_64 arm64e arm64e.x1'", thinned x86_64 -> "'x86_64'", thinned arm64e -> 'arm64e', 16-byte file with cffaedfe magic -> 'lipo cannot read ... lipo: not a mach-o', text-only stage -> 'nothing executable was staged'. CLI mode matches on a file, a directory, an archive, and refuses `release.sh` itself ('not a Mach-O, an archive or a directory'). 19/19 arms behave under bash 5.3.20 **and** under /bin/bash 3.2.57 (rc=0 both). Gates: `tools/lint.sh shellcheck` ok (0.11.0, 27 scripts), `tools/lint.sh shell` ok (system bash 3.2.57, 27 scripts) - the SC1090 on the runtime-derived `source` is closed with `# shellcheck source=/dev/null`, which was verified to be the directive doing the work, not a silently ignored one.

Two things this batch did NOT confirm, stated rather than smoothed over: (1) a full `tools/release.sh --dry-run` is **not checked** - its precondition chain demands the tag be pushed, and 'do not push yet' is in force, so call-site reachability is proven on the script's own extracted lines instead of on a whole run. (2) The row's prepared expectation asked for the **demo binary** in the library stage; measured, there is none - `tools/build_library.sh` ships `demo/main.swift` plus `build-static.sh` and `build-dynamic.sh`, source and scripts only. The library archive's 2 Mach-O are the .a and the .dylib, so the guard covers what actually ships, and the expectation was wrong, not the fix.

Sibling defect found and fixed in the same batch (5a195d8): the engine archive had no per-product membership assertion. `release.sh` runs `set -uo pipefail` without errexit, so a failing `cp` is silent, and the stage loop's `[ -x "$BIN/$p" ]` is true for a *directory*, which `cp` then skips with 'is a directory (not copied)'. A release could therefore ship three binaries under a name promising four - and the new arch count would have reported '3 Mach-O artifacts' as if that were the specification. The loop now requires each of the four products by name inside the tar, which is what makes the count mean four rather than 'whatever arrived'.

tasks.title: A quantized weight width outside [4, 8] is accepted by the CPU snapshot reader, and the one place that did route a 6-bit width could only abort the process
tasks.category: input validation at a trust boundary (width reaches kernel arithmetic)
tasks.discovered-by: AUD-159 fix, sibling sweep (which other numbers read from a file reach arithmetic unasked?)
tasks.evidence-before:
The width is not a preference. Kernels derive their addressing from it: `AffineQuant`/`SlotGEMV`/`MoE`/`MPPPrefillInt4QMM`/`PrefillGroupedRoutedMoE`/`PrefillPrimitives`/`PrefillFinalRowHead` all carry `precondition([4, 8].contains(weightBits))` (AffineQuant.swift:48 and :131, SlotGEMV.swift:30-32, MoE.swift:134, MPPPrefillInt4QMM.swift:34, PrefillGroupedRoutedMoE.swift:208, PrefillPrimitives.swift:8 and :98, PrefillFinalRowHead.swift:14); the CPU path either dies on purpose (`CPUTensorOps.swift:154` `preconditionFailure("no CPU kernel for \(matrix.bits)-bit weights")`) or divides by it in silence (`CPUQwen35+Quant.swift:16` `let lanes = 32 / matrix.bits` -- at 6 bits that is 5 lanes, and the same bytes unpack to plausible nonsense). Measured rather than argued: a throwaway test constructing `AffineQuantGEMV` at 6 bits exited with signal 5 on `TinyTitan/AffineQuant.swift:48: Precondition failed`; the probe was then deleted.
Per route: (1) GPU manifest -- already gated twice: a slot width is refused at manifest read (`ManifestReader.validateQuant`, ManifestReader.swift:256-265) and a per-tensor override is refused while decoding (`SSDAIManifestQuantV1.init(from:)`, SSDAIManifestV1.swift:248-258). **This part of the report was not true**: my first hypothesis was that overrides were ungated on the GPU route; a `Model.validateOverrideWidths` gate was written against that hypothesis, the decoder guard was then found, and both edits were fully reverted -- the honest residue is that a real guard had **no test**: `grep -rnE "quant override for|supportedWeightBits|bits; supported" tests/` returned nothing. (2) CPU snapshot (`config.json`) -- the live hole. `AffineSnapshot` read `quantization.bits` and every per-tensor override with `as? Int` casts and no range check at any point before the width reached `dequantize` and the GEMV dispatch. (3) The CPU `.ssdai` route shares the gated decoder. (4) `SharedExpertAffineQuant.swift` (73 lines) was a 6-bit-only composition whose **single** construction site passed `weightBits: 6` into `AffineQuantGEMV`, which asserts [4, 8] -- so `SharedExpertInt4`'s `case 6:` arm could not produce output or an error, only a trap; 6-bit is a withdrawn format per AGENTS.md, so the arm was dead code whose only reachable behaviour was a crash.
tasks.fix-summary: The gate moved to where the width is read, and the dead arm was deleted. `AffineSnapshot.validateWidths(baseBits:widths:)` (new, sources/TinyTitan/CPUEngine/AffineSnapshot.swift) checks the declared base width **and** every per-tensor override -- sorted, so the refusal is deterministic -- and throws `SafeTensorsFile.Failure.malformed("... declares N-bit weights. The CPU kernels implement 4 and 8 only, so this snapshot cannot be read correctly -- not as a reference and not as output.")`. It is called from the safetensors/`config.json` initializer only; the `.ssdai` initializer documents why it does not need it (the decoder already refused), rather than adding a second, differently-worded check of the same fact. `SharedExpertAffineQuant.swift` is deleted and `SharedExpertInt4` loses its `.affine` case, its `case 6:` and the encode arm, leaving `default: throw SharedExpertError.unsupportedWeightBits(weightBits)` -- an error, naming the width, instead of a trap. The comment at the switch records which two guards keep an unsupported width from ever arriving. Tests: `tests/TinyTitan/Kernels/MoE/SharedExpertRuntimeTests.swift` (new) pins 4 and 8 building and 6/3/16/0/32 throwing with the width both in the case payload and in `error.description`; `ManifestReaderTests` gains the first test of the pre-existing override decode guard, at 6/3/16/2 bits, asserting the message names the tensor stem; `CPUEngineTests` gains base-width and override-width arms through the real `AffineSnapshot(directory:)` loader.
tasks.evidence-after:
Corrections first: the row's own first hypothesis (GPU per-tensor overrides ungated) was **not true**, and the code written for it was reverted before commit -- `git status` on `Model+Validation.swift` and `Model+SchemaValidation.swift` is clean, which is the evidence that it is reverted and not merely described as so.
The trap claim is measured: signal 5 with `TinyTitan/AffineQuant.swift:48: Precondition failed` from a throwaway test, not an assertion about preconditions.
Every new assertion was mutation-checked, reverted, and re-verified green. M1 -- delete the `AffineSnapshot.validateWidths` call site: exactly 4 issues in `CPUEngineTests` (34 pass after restoring). M2 -- make the decoder's width guard `guard true`: exactly the 4 new decode assertions fail, on "a 6-bit override must not decode" and its siblings; restored from /tmp/ssdai-m2.bak. M3 -- return `.dimensionMismatch` instead of `.unsupportedWeightBits`: all 5 widths caught; restored from /tmp/se-m3.bak.
`swift test --no-parallel --filter` over the three affected suites: 69 tests in 5 suites, 0 failures. Full package suite on the committed tree: `swift test --no-parallel`, **1668 tests in 229 suites across 7 bundles, 0 failures, exit 0** (/tmp/aud161-full.log; the deleted class and the removed arm leave no dangling reference -- `grep -rn SharedExpertAffineQuant sources/ tests/` returns nothing).
Gates on the committed tree: `tools/lint.sh` swift-format, swiftlint, force-cast, func-length, file-length, unbounded-read, sendable -- all pass.
Sibling sweep, and what it found: the GPU route, the CPU `.ssdai` route, the repack/verification route (`PackedExpertWidthTests`) and the server/lib width reporting (`identity.weightBits`, and `routedExpertWeightBits` which comes from a slot) are all behind one of the two gates. Two honest observations: `validateRoleUniformity`'s `bits == 16` allowance for the GDN a/b pair is **unreachable from a manifest**, because the decoder refuses 16 -- harmless, but it is a branch no input can take; and `CPUTensorOps.swift:154`'s `preconditionFailure` is deliberately kept as the last-resort guard now that the width is refused at load, since converting it to a throw would move the check to every call site. Not checked, stated: no golden-baseline or model run, because no supported install is 6-bit (it is a withdrawn format) and `models/` holds only the two Qwen3.8 4-bit installs -- this route is reachable only from a hand-supplied snapshot directory, which the new tests build synthetically.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitan/CPUEngine/AffineSnapshot.swift:205 (the fenced open loop, formerly an unguarded appendPathComponent), sources/TinyTitan/CPUEngine/SafeTensors.swift:80 (the O_NOFOLLOW opener)
tasks.title: The CPU snapshot opens every shard name it reads out of the model index with no containment and no O_NOFOLLOW, while three sibling loaders fence the same contract
tasks.category: trusting manifest content: the boundary fenced everywhere else is unfenced on one path
tasks.discovered-by: the L4 security sweep over names and bytes that come from outside this process
tasks.evidence-before: An installed model directory can arrive copied off another machine, so an index's `weight_map` values are external input, not a list this process wrote. The CPU loader turned each one straight into `directory.appendingPathComponent(file)` and handed the URL to `SafeTensorsFile(url:)`, whose opener was a plain `open(O_RDONLY)`: no canonicalisation, so `../../...` resolved out of the snapshot, and no `O_NOFOLLOW`, so a symlink at a plausible shard name mapped a file outside the directory into the engine's address space. `SSDAIModelDirectory` already fences both halves (a non-canonical name is refused, every component opens `O_NOFOLLOW` relative to the directory's own descriptor), `LocalSnapshotLoader` fences the same contract for the other engine, and the `.ssdai` path fences it again -- three siblings and one hole. The hole is on the CPU path, which is the one a user reaches for when the GPU path will not fit.
tasks.fix-summary: The shard loop opens through `SSDAIModelDirectory(rootURL:)` the way its siblings do, so containment is checked per name and every component opens relative to the snapshot's own descriptor. `SafeTensorsFile` gains an init that adopts an already-open descriptor, because opening by name and then re-opening by URL is a TOCTOU: the bytes mapped must be the bytes that were checked. The URL init now sets `O_NOFOLLOW` itself, so the fence lives in the opener and a caller cannot forget it.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06 during the L4 pass. 4 tests in `tests/TinyTitan/CPUEngine/CPUEngineTests.swift`: `aShardNameThatEscapesTheSnapshotIsRefused`, `aSymlinkedShardIsRefusedRatherThanMapped`, `aSymlinkedURLIsRefusedByTheOpener`, and AUD-165's bound test. Against the pre-fix sources all four fail with `an error was expected but none was thrown`, so each binds to the fence rather than to the fixture. The full CPU suite is 38 tests in 2 suites, passed, re-run after the fix commits. NOT covered as filed: `AffineSnapshot.swift` was at exactly 500 physical lines, the `file-length` ceiling with no headroom, so the next change to the file had to split it along a seam first. That is what 75501ed did: the two loaders and `fullAttentionInterval(of:)` moved to `AffineSnapshot+Loading.swift` as pure code motion, 231 added lines against 219 removed -- the difference is the new file's `import Foundation`, its header and the extension brace.

tasks.title: POST /v1/models/unload has no browser-form gate, so a form POST from any LAN page can reach the route that unloads the resident model
tasks.category: half-covered guard: five mutating routes check the content type and the sixth does not
tasks.discovered-by: enumerating which routes the AUD-147 Origin/content-type guards actually reach
tasks.evidence-before: `/v1/models/unload` read its body through the absent-content-type-tolerant helper rather than the gated path, so an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or `multipart/form-data` POST -- what a browser sends from a plain `<form>` with no preflight to answer for it -- reached the route whose only effect is to drop the loaded model. The other five mutating JSON routes all carry the gate. The helper could not simply be swapped: its absent-header permissiveness is the CLI's contract, which is the AUD-132 lesson, so the route needed the guard rather than a stricter body reader. Nothing in the suite had ever sent a non-JSON content type to any of the five that do carry the gate, so the missing sixth had no test to fail and the guard was pinned only by memory.
tasks.fix-summary: `notAForm` is computed once at the top of the route table and the unload case guards on it, answering 415 through the same `writeUnsupportedMediaType` the other five use, so the envelope stays per-surface instead of inventing a new error shape.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. `unloadRefusesABrowserFormPost` drives three form encodings at the live route and asserts 415 and that the body does not say `unloaded`. `everyJsonRouteRefusesANonJsonContentType` pins the gate on all five gated routes at once and checks the two surfaces apart because they answer apart: the OpenAI envelope carries `unsupported_media_type` and the Anthropic one is `invalid_request_error` with no code field at all -- the first draft read that as a missing gate until it printed the body. The encoder escapes the slash in `application/json`, so the message assertion stops before it. `HTTPServerTests` is 22/22 passed.

tasks.file_line: plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/peers.js:103 (the counted reader), sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetClient.swift:113 (the counted byte loop)
tasks.title: Both peer readers buffer whatever a host sends them, so the LAN prober can be sized by any host inside its own fence and held open indefinitely
tasks.category: unbounded receive on a discovery path, in two languages
tasks.discovered-by: the L4 pass over every place this tree reads a socket it did not choose
tasks.evidence-before: `probe()` dials every candidate the fence admits and buffered the whole response before parsing. The default fence includes the self-assigned range, so any host on the local link without a DHCP address is a candidate, and it only has to answer `{ok: true}` to be believed a member -- the group field is how a peer says which fleet it is in, not a credential. Two costs, both paid by the resident manager: memory grows with whatever the peer chooses to send, and the JS socket `timeout` is an inactivity timer, so a peer that keeps writing is never cut off. `URLSessionTransport` on the Swift side had the same shape through `data(for:)`, which buffers the whole body before the caller sees a byte count.
tasks.fix-summary: Both readers count as bytes arrive and stop at a declared cap: `MAX_PEER_RESPONSE_BYTES` is exported from `peers.js` so a test can name the rule it enforces, and an over-cap answer destroys the request with the cap in the message. `FleetClient` carries the same 4 MiB as `static let maxResponseBytes` and a new `FleetError.responseTooLarge(target:bytes:)` that says who was too large. The Swift loop stays byte-at-a-time: `chunks(ofCount:)` measured absent on `URLSession.AsyncBytes` at this SDK, so the comment records the measurement instead of an assumed optimisation.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. Both tests run against a real loopback server, because the guard is inside the response reader and a stubbed `fetch` cannot reach it. JS (`test/peers.test.js`): the under-cap inventory still parses and the never-ending over-cap answer is refused; the first version hung rather than failing on the unfixed code, which was itself the second half of this defect, so the test carries an 8 s unref'd deadline that turns the regression into an observable failure. Swift (`tests/TinyTitanFleet/ResponseBoundTests.swift`): the first socket test in that target, over a raw POSIX loopback server -- `sin_len` and the `in_addr` byte order were both wrong in the first draft, and the failure now carries `errno` so the next one is diagnosable. Full suites after the fix: fleet 49 tests in 13 suites passed, plugin `npm test` 129 passed / 0 failed. NOT covered as filed: the sentence claimed the cap bounds one answer "not the number of concurrent probes", and the second half was wrong -- the probes are bounded, at DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY 24 (peers.js:36, :433-437) with a shallower 4 for the hostname-resolution phase (:417), and mapLimit's own bound and ordering are tested (test/peers.test.js:79-95). What was genuinely unpinned is the wiring at :435, and that became AUD-173; the size cap and the fan-out cap together are what keep one prober from being sized by the LAN.

tasks.file_line: tools/dsh_route.sh (the --from-server served-id block)
tasks.title: The route validator prints model ids it reads off a running server straight into the settings block, where both sibling writers validate the same field
tasks.category: trusting an id read from the network on one writer and validating it on two
tasks.discovered-by: comparing the three writers of the same settings block against each other
tasks.evidence-before: `--from-server` asks a live server for `/v1/models` and writes each id verbatim into the YAML block it emits. The catalogue parser refuses an empty or multi-line field and the plugin writer runs the same validator over its own input; this path asked neither question, on the theory that a running server only names real models. An id carrying a newline became two rows in the block, and one carrying YAML punctuation changed what the block declares rather than what it names. The failure was also invisible: the python check raised into a command substitution whose stderr was not the launcher's, so the operator saw `listed no models` instead of the reason.
tasks.fix-summary: Every served id must match `[A-Za-z0-9._-]+` before anything is printed, the refusal captures the validator's stderr and passes it to `die`, and nothing is emitted unless the whole listing passes -- so a refusal leaves the array empty and the existing empty-listing error still fires.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. 4 tests in `benchmark/test_dsh_route.py` (`ServedIdTests`) drive a real `ThreadingHTTPServer` on 127.0.0.1 port 0 rather than a stub, because the claim is what the shell does with a live answer: plain ids reach the block, an id with a newline is refused, an id with YAML punctuation is refused, and one bad id refuses the whole listing. Suite: 17 passed including the 4 new. `tools/lint.sh shell` and `shellcheck` clean, and the loop is a `while read` rather than `mapfile` because /bin/bash on a factory Mac is 3.2.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanFleet/Command/main.swift:115 (was the inline `??` chain), sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift
tasks.title: `ttlanmanager --key` puts the group key in argv, where every other local account reads it with ps, and nothing said so
tasks.category: secret through a world-visible channel, on the one path where the secret is the operator's own
tasks.discovered-by: the L4 sweep's leftover question about how the fleet key is carried
tasks.evidence-before: The shipped default `tinytitan-lan` is public by design -- `router.js:101` tells a peer that presents it that the key `groups rather than protects`, and that is the right reading of a default. So the key that matters is the one an operator chose *because* they want other people out, and the documented way to pass it to the CLI is `--key`, which is also the first name in the resolution order the help text prints. macOS shows every account's argv to every other account through `ps`; a process's environment belongs to its own user. The help line named the order and never named the difference, and the README's own habit of writing the token into a `curl -H` argument goes out the same door. Nothing in the tree said which spelling to prefer.
tasks.fix-summary: The resolution moves out of the executable's top-level code into `FleetGroupKey` -- `FleetKey` was already taken by the keyboard enum in `FleetDashboard.swift` -- with the order untouched, and returns the warning alongside the key. `--key` now puts one line on stderr naming the channel and pointing at `DSH_LAN_KEY`, and the usage text says the same before anyone types it. Errors and warnings go to stderr, so `--json` output stays parseable.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. 2 tests in `tests/TinyTitanFleet/KeySourceTests.swift` pin both the warning and the order (a reorder would change which key a machine presents without touching any other assertion). Fleet suite 51 tests in 13 suites passed. Mutation probe: with the warning replaced by `nil` the test fails with two named issues, so the probe is not a compile check. Live: `swift run ttlanmanager --key probe-key --peer 127.0.0.1:59999 --timeout 1 inventory` prints the line on stderr before dialling anything, and the executable builds under `-warnings-as-errors`. NOT covered as filed: the same literal lives in `plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/config.js` as `DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY` and nothing pinned the two together -- a Swift test reaching into `plugins/` has no precedent here, and inventing one was not this row's call. AUD-175 (c3b3a84) closed it from the other side, in `tools/docs-facts.py`, which is allowed to read both languages.

tasks.file_line: plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/router.js:326 (the catch-all), plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/api.js:800 (the session-controller wrapper)
tasks.title: An unexpected throw answers with its own message, so a filesystem failure names this Mac's paths to any peer that can reach the port
tasks.category: internal detail in an error answer, plus a mislabelled status on the sibling site
tasks.discovered-by: the L4 pass over what the manager says when it fails
tasks.evidence-before: The router's catch-all answered 500 with `error.message` verbatim. The throws that reach it are the unexpected ones -- `node:fs` and child-process failures -- and Node puts the absolute path in their messages, so the answer told any caller where this Mac keeps its profiles. The manager listens on the LAN by design, so "any caller" is not only this user. One layer down sat the same defect with a second problem: the session-controller wrapper wrapped *any* throw into an `ApiError` carrying its message, so that route never passed through the router fence at all, and its fallback gave an uncoded controller failure status 400 -- telling the caller to fix a request that was fine.
tasks.fix-summary: The catch-all keeps the log line that already recorded the stack and answers with a fixed message that says where the detail is. `ApiError` messages still go out unchanged, because those are authored here and are the documented answer for a known failure. The wrapper now keeps the code and message only of an error the controller *authored* -- one carrying its own code -- and rethrows anything else to the catch-all, which both logs it and calls it a 500.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. `an unexpected throw answers a fixed 500 and keeps its detail in the log` asserts the absence of the path and the presence of the log line, so the fix cannot become a silent failure. On the unfixed sources it fails with `expected: 500` and an actual of 400 -- the path was in the body at that point. Suite 130 pass / 0 fail; the 501 case and the `workspace/not-found` case still assert their authored messages, which is the half that had to survive. NOT covered as filed: the fan-out receipts in `prompt-all` and the archive path echo per-session failure messages, and api.js has no logger in scope to put the detail anywhere else -- fixing that needs a log channel threaded through, not a message swapped. That is what AUD-174 (cf2088d) then did, at all six sites this class has here.

tasks.file_line: plugins/dsh-tinytitan/src/route.js:77 (registerRoute), plugins/dsh-tinytitan/src/generate.js:476 (repairDefaultModelSettings)
tasks.title: Neither settings-file route writer repoints agent-default-model, so a profile without a settings service gets the stale-default failure AUD-163 closed
tasks.category: stale configuration reference after a refresh
tasks.discovered-by: the L6 closure sweep, which re-read every row's NOT-covered sentence against the current code rather than trusting it
tasks.evidence-before: AUD-163's own caveat named this branch and said it was not covered: "the pre-0.2.0 file path (`generateRoute`/`writeRouteSettings`, reached when a harness has no settings service) still writes only `llm-pi-ai` and inherits the same stale-default defect." Checked, and live. `index.js` picks the writer by whether the profile composes a settings service (:122 `legacy = registerRoute`, called at :212 via `ctx.inject(["settings"], ...)`), and on a profile that answers no `settings` the legacy writer runs instead. Both of its halves refresh only the route: the shell branch executes `tools/dsh_route.sh --write`, and `generateRoute`/`writeRouteSettings` rewrite the `llm-pi-ai` section. Nothing on that path ever read `agent-default-model`. Consequence, the same as AUD-163's: after the operator changed which model is installed the refresh updated the picker, the window showed the live model, every turn went out naming the dead id and came back `pi-ai provider "tinytitan" has no configured model <id>` / `UNKNOWN_MODEL`, and the profile looked correctly configured the whole time. `ensureDefaultModel` -- the repair -- was reachable only from `applyRouteThroughSettings`, i.e. only on the branch the pinned harness takes, which is why 144 green tests never saw the other one.
tasks.fix-summary: The repair moved out of the service call and next to both file writes. `applyDefaultModelToSettings` is the pure half: it reads the served ids back out of the `llm-pi-ai` block in the file (`servedIdsInLines`), which is what the writer just wrote, so one implementation works after either the shell tool or the built-in generator refreshed it; it returns `repaired`/`kept`/`skipped` with the reason, and rewrites only the one `model:` line, to the first served id. `repairDefaultModelSettings` is the file half and shares the new `replaceSettingsFile` with `writeRouteSettings`, so a refresh and a repair cannot disagree about whether a no-op makes a `.bak-*`; its stamp carries a `-default` suffix so its backup of the same file cannot clobber the route write's backup. `registerRoute` calls it through `repairDefaultAfterWrite` after each of the two success branches and adds the outcome to the result as `defaultModel`, the field the service branch already returns. The rule stays as narrow as AUD-163's, for the stated reason: this edits somebody else's profile, so a default naming a served model is a choice, a default belonging to another provider is a choice, and a default that was never set is `dsh_local.sh`'s job -- only a reference this repository wrote and can prove dead is rewritten. A repair failure never fails the refresh: the route is already on disk and turning `written` into `failed` would push the caller down the "leaving the route as it is" path over a smaller, separate defect, so the reason goes to the log.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. Probe first, on the pre-fix sources: a standalone driver of `registerRoute`'s script branch against a profile whose route serves `alpha_4-Bit` and whose default names `gone_4-Bit`, run with `src/generate.js` and `src/route.js` restored from `git show HEAD:` (backed up to /tmp first, then put back and confirmed by `git diff`) -- it fails with `AssertionError: no default repair ran on the file branch / actual undefined, expected 'repaired'`, exit 1. The same driver passes on the fixed sources. 10 unit and integration tests added: the pure rule over all six outcomes, the block found on either side of the route (the scan stops at the next column-0 key, so a default below `llm-pi-ai:` must be read as carefully as one above), the write-once-and-back-up and no-op-makes-no-backup behaviour over a real file, both writers' integration (built-in generator, and the script branch with an injected `run`), and `chmod 0o000` on the settings file to show a repair that cannot write still returns `written` with the reason logged. Suites after: dsh-tinytitan `npm test` 154 passed / 0 failed (was 144), `tools/lint.sh javascript` ok on the pinned eslint 10.11.0 / prettier 3.9.9 -- it failed once on an unused binding in the new tests before it passed, so the gate is live. NOT covered: the shell branch's repair is pinned against an injected `run`, so it proves what `registerRoute` does with the file after the tool exits, not that `dsh_route.sh` wrote a valid block -- that half is AUD-157's checkout-tool comparison.

tasks.file_line: plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/peers.js:435 (the untested limit argument)
tasks.title: The peer prober's fan-out bound is applied but pinned by no test, so deleting it leaves the whole suite green
tasks.category: unpinned guard (missing test)
tasks.discovered-by: the L6 closure sweep, while checking whether AUD-168's NOT-covered sentence was still true
tasks.evidence-before: AUD-168 closed the size of one peer's answer and said the number of concurrent probes was not covered. It is covered by code: `#refresh()` fans probes out through `mapLimit(validated, this.config.discoveryConcurrency ?? DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, ...)` (peers.js:433-437) with `DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY = 24` (:36), and the resolution phase runs on its own shallower `?? 4` (:417) which does have a test (test/peers.test.js:312-333). What had no witness was the argument at :435: `mapLimit` itself is tested for bound and order (:79-95), and `discoveryConcurrency` is validated in config.js:216-218, but nothing asserted that either reaches the probe fan-out. Mutation-measured: replacing that expression with `validated.length` leaves all 130 other tests in the file passing while the resident manager dials every candidate the fence admits at once -- 24 sockets held open per cycle becomes as many as discovery returns.
tasks.fix-summary: One test that counts peak in-flight fetches across a refresh: over 40 candidates with no configured limit it must be exactly `DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY`, and over 12 with `discoveryConcurrency: 3` it must be exactly 3. The second case is what makes the first mean "the configured limit is applied" rather than "some number happened to be peak"; `===` rather than `<=` because a bound that silently became 1 would be a different defect (a cycle that never finishes) and an inequality would let it pass as a success.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-06. With `peers.js:435` mutated to `validated.length` the new test fails (peak 40, expected 24) and is the only failure; `src/peers.js` was then restored from a copy taken before the edit and `git diff` reports no change, i.e. the committed source is untouched -- only the test file is in the commit. Full suites after: dsh-lan-manager `npm test` 131 passed / 0 failed, `tools/lint.sh javascript` ok.

tasks.file_line: plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/api.js:547,563,692,743,847 (the interpolated messages) and :814 (the authored-code test)
tasks.title: The sites AUD-171 left open answer a LAN peer with the harness's own failure text, and the one that meant to keep only authored failures admits a Node error code
tasks.category: internal detail in an error answer (information disclosure)
tasks.discovered-by: the L6 closure sweep, following the NOT-covered sentence filed in the AUD-173 row, which named exactly these sites
tasks.evidence-before: At 9c98268 six places put a failure this process did not author into an answer any peer inside the address fence can ask for. `derivedMessagesFromStore` interpolated the caught error's message into two 503s (`…could not be read from storage: ENOENT…` at :547, `…could not be prepared for reading: ENOENT…` at :563); `promptAllActive`'s per-session receipt carried it verbatim (:692); `deleteWorkspace`'s `archiveFailures` carried it with no code at all (:741-744); `createWorkspace` answered 400 with the caught message as the whole answer (:845-848). The sixth is the same class in a different shape: `startSession` keeps a caught error's code and message when `typeof error?.code === "string"` (:814) -- and a Node error has a string `code` too (`ENOENT`, `EACCES`), so a failed spawn's `child_process` text goes out labelled a caller's bad request. Reproduced, not argued: the seven tests added with this fix were run against `git show 9c98268:` copies of `src/api.js` and `src/router.js` (swapped in, restored afterwards, tree confirmed clean) and 6 of 7 fail there with the leak printed in the assertion output -- e.g. `{"error":"agent-service-unavailable","message":"session s-a1 could not be read from storage: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/Users/me/.dsh/home/profiles/web/s-a1.json'"}`, `{"sessionId":"s-b1","code":"error","message":"ENOENT: …s-b1.json"}`, and `400 !== 500` for the spawn failure. AUD-171 had already recorded that these sites were left open because none of them held a logger.
tasks.fix-summary: One rule, applied at all six: the code and the status are the documented answer and stay; the reason goes to the manager's log. `loggedApiError` builds the ApiError from a sentence authored here plus `; the reason is in the manager's log`, and `loggedReceipt` does the same for a fan-out entry while keeping that failure's declared `code` -- which also gives `archiveFailures` a code it never had. The log channel is threaded `createHandler` -> `dispatch` -> the four operations as a **separate trailing `plumbing` argument**, not inside `options`: `options` is the request body's shape and a peer must not be able to hand the plugin a function. `startSession`'s authored-code test becomes `isDocumentedCode`, which accepts the lowercase-hyphen, optionally namespaced vocabulary this plugin and the harness actually emit (`not-found`, `workspace/not-found`, `session-busy`) and rethrows an uppercase Node code so the router's catch-all logs it and answers a fixed 500 -- the status also stops calling an internal failure the caller's bad request. The message rule is now written down in the plugin README's Security section, next to the key-never-in-a-response rule.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-07 on commit cf2088d. Seven tests in `test/router.test.js`: one per leaking site, and each of those six asserts the answer carries no `/Users/me` **and** that the reason reached the injected log -- so a guard that only moved the leak would still fail. The seventh is the counter-test, deliberately passing before and after -- `an authored ApiError still says what it means inside a fan-out` asserts `session s-a2 has no live agent (start it in the UI, then retry)` still arrives, because fencing somebody else's text must not turn every answer into a shrug; it is why the negative probe shows 6 failures and not 7. Suite: `npm test` in dsh-lan-manager reports 138 tests / 138 pass / 0 fail (was 131 before these seven), dsh-tinytitan 154/154, and `tools/lint.sh javascript` reports ok for both packages on the pinned eslint 10.11.0 / prettier 3.9.9. The negative probe is above; after restoring, `git status --short` on the package is empty and both files matched their pre-probe checksums.

tasks.file_line: tools/docs-facts.py: shared_group_key(), called from main(). The two definitional sites it reads: sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift:20 (shippedDefault) and plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/config.js:54 (DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY)
tasks.title: The shipped fleet group key is one value written in two languages, and a drift between them empties every peer table without failing any gate
tasks.category: two sources of truth for one identity fact, with prose as the only link
tasks.discovered-by: the L6 closure sweep, following the NOT-covered sentence filed in the AUD-170 row, which named this literal and the JS one beside it
tasks.evidence-before: Written twice by necessity, pinned by nothing. `FleetGroupKey.shippedDefault` is `"tinytitan-lan"` in Swift and `DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY` is the same string in the plugin's `config.js`, because one Mac runs the CLI and the harness side against one LAN and an unconfigured install must present the *same key* to both. The only link was prose: the Swift doc comment's "the two literals here have to move with it" and the resolution-order row in `config.js`'s module header. The consequence of moving one is quiet, not loud. A member names its group by a digest of the key it presents (`groupDigest`, AUD-154), so a machine on the changed default computes a different digest, `router.js` answers it as a foreign group, and the peer table empties -- no error, no non-zero exit, nothing in a log that says *your fleet has no members because your default moved*. Measured on the pre-fix tree (8686e9e): with `config.js` edited to `"tinytitan-la"` -- one character short of the Swift literal -- `python3 tools/docs-facts.py` printed `ok (83 documents against 17 gates ...)` and exited 0. Every gate here reads either its own language or its own file; none had ever looked at both.
tasks.fix-summary: `shared_group_key()` in the docs gate reads both definitional sites by pattern, not by quoting a value into a document, and returns a row for each way it can go wrong: `FAIL cannot read <rel> for the group key: ...`, `FAIL <rel>: no shipped default group key matched <pattern>`, and `FAIL the shipped group key has two values: <site> = <value>; ...`. The middle one is the important shape -- a renamed or reformatted declaration fails the gate instead of leaving a site unchecked, which is the rule this file already applies to its own counter (`docs` reports a failure when it derived no gates). Both literals now carry a line naming the pin, and the `docs` bullet in `AGENTS.md` says the gate reads a value defined in two languages, so the next person who edits one finds the fence before the drift.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-07 on commit c3b3a84. Two mutation probes, each failing observably, each restored and verified by checksum with `git status` clean afterwards. Drifting the JS literal by one character: `FAIL the shipped group key has two values: plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/config.js = 'tinytitan-la'; sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift = 'tinytitan-lan'`. Re-spelling the Swift declaration as `public static let shippedDefault: String = { "tinytitan-lan" }()`, which compiles and behaves identically: `FAIL sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift: no shipped default group key matched static let shippedDefault = "([^"]+)"` -- so the check cannot be quietly disarmed by editing its own pattern out of the source. Restored tree: `docs` ok on 83 documents against 17 derived gates, exit 0. `python` (ruff 0.16.7, parses under 3.13), `swift-format`, `swiftlint --strict`, `file-length` (largest 496) and `javascript` (eslint 10.11.0 + prettier 3.9.9, suite 138 pass / 0 fail) clean; `swift build` and the Fleet suite (51 tests in 13 suites, `--no-parallel`) pass. NOT covered: the check pins the two *shipped defaults* to each other, not either to the fleet's real configuration -- an operator who sets `DSH_LAN_KEY` on some members and not others still gets an empty peer table, correctly, and no gate here can know which keys were meant to match. Also not covered: `config.js:166`'s resolution order (`groupKey ?? token ?? DSH_LAN_KEY ?? DSH_LAN_TOKEN ?? DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY`) is the mirror of the Swift order AUD-170 pinned in `KeySourceTests.swift`, and the two orders are still kept in step by reading them, not by a check.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanServer/Core/CPUModelBackend.swift:189-195 (the sampler built from the config) and sources/TinyTitan/CPUEngine/CPUSampler.swift:15-31 (the shape it could hold)
tasks.title: The CPU serving path accepts `seed`, `presence_penalty` and `repetition_penalty`, applies none of them, and is the engine meant to check the GPU path with
tasks.category: documented API accepted then dropped on one of two engines, so the same request answers differently with nothing said
tasks.discovered-by: the L7/section-5 pass, looking for a second implementation of generation that had drifted from the first -- AGENTS rule 2 says a front end that reimplements sampling is drift, and here it had
tasks.evidence-before: The validator is shared: `OpenAIRequestValidator.swift:194-195,276-280` puts `presencePenalty`, `repetitionPenalty` and `seed` on one `GenerationConfig` for every entry, GPU or CPU. The GPU sampler reads all three -- `Runtime/Generation/Sampler.swift:83-93` applies both penalties before the kernel sees the row, and `:294-299` `seedFor(config:position:)` honours `config.seed` -- while the CPU backend at 7cee919's parent built `CPUSampler(temperature:topP:topK:seed:)` from a `CPUSampler` struct that has no penalty fields at all, and set the seed with `configuration.temperature > 0 ? nil : 0`. `grep -n 'presencePenalty|repetitionPenalty|\.seed'` over the whole backend returned nothing. The consequence is not only a request that asks for `presence_penalty: 1.5` and does not get it -- it is a model row that publishes it: `GenerationDefaults.qwen38Instruct` carries `presencePenalty: 1.5` (`SamplerTypes.swift:55-57`), so serving a non-thinking Qwen3.8 request on CPU silently removes a penalty the checkpoint specifies. And this engine exists to be an independent reference for the GPU one (`docs/plan-cpu-side-engine.md`), so a dropped penalty is the comparison disagreeing for a reason that is in neither model. No document said the CPU path was penalty-free, and `--cpu` is a usage-text flag (`ServerArguments+Usage.swift:105`), not a debug switch. Nothing in `tests/` covered the sampled CPU path at all: `CPUModelBackendTests` generated once, at `temperature: 0`.
tasks.fix-summary: `CPUSampler` carries both penalties and applies them the way the GPU sampler does, minus its softcap branch because this engine has no softcap: a distinct id in the history is divided by the repetition factor while its logit is positive and multiplied while negative, then has the presence penalty subtracted -- before the argmax, so greedy respects them too, as the GPU's greedy does. An id outside the row is skipped rather than trapping. The backend seeds the history with the prompt ids and appends each produced token, because the prompt is in the model's context and the GPU caller passes the same thing, and it takes the request's seed instead of deriving one from the temperature. tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanMemoryTool/main.swift:126-136 (the `forget` branch at ea0c4f1)
tasks.title: `tinytitan-memory forget --yes` deletes a workspace a running server holds, and deletes the lock file that server is writing through
tasks.category: documented refusal not implemented, on the one command that destroys a whole project
tasks.discovered-by: the L7/ops pass, reading each of the tool's five commands against the promise its own usage header makes -- the header says `delete` and `forget` refuse a held workspace, and only one of them did
tasks.evidence-before: `main.swift:15-16` says "Reads take no lock and work while a server is running; delete and forget need the workspace, and refuse it while a server holds it", and `docs/agent-memory.md:370-373` repeats it to the operator. The `delete` path gets its refusal from `FileJournal(url:)` at `main.swift:141`, which raises `JournalError.locked` (`ContinuityCore/Persistence/Journal.swift:143-146`, `flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)`) and is turned into that message at `:142`. The `forget` branch had no such open: `try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: file.url.appendingPathExtension("lock"))` then `removeItem(at: file.url)`, printing `forgot <project>` and `exit(0)` -- and the `try?` on the sidecar means even a failed unlink is silent. The consequence is written on `MemoryService.isLockHeld` (`sources/TinyTitanMemory/MemoryService+Maintenance.swift:15-18`): "Deleting a file another process is appending to takes its `.lock` with it -- the file that process's `flock` is attached to -- and leaves it writing to a deleted inode, which its next compaction then rewrites into nothing." So this is not a stale file left behind: the next compaction by the live server replaces the project on disk with whatever that server holds in RAM, and the operator has been told the project was forgotten. `MemoryService.isLockHeld` is `internal`, so the tool target cannot reach it; `FileJournal` is `public actor` (`Journal.swift:21`) and is the idiom the same file already uses. No test covered `forget` at all, and none could have reached it as a unit: the target is an executable with no library behind it, so it needs a subprocess test, and `tests/TinyTitanMemory/` had none.
tasks.fix-summary: The branch opens the journal before removing anything, and keeps that object alive across both removals with `withExtendedLifetime` rather than probing the lock and dropping it -- a launch that slipped between a probe and the unlink would land on the same deleted-inode path the fence exists to prevent. The refusal names what to do (`Stop the server that has this project open, or forget through it.`), matching the shape of the `delete` path's message. The sidecar unlink is no longer `try?`: it sits in the same `do`, so a failed unlink is a `could not delete:` refusal rather than a partial forget reported as success. The order is unchanged (journal, then sidecar) and the sidecar is still derived from `file.url` -- `FileJournal.url` is actor-isolated, which the compiler caught rather than the test.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured 2026-10-07 on 74413ba. New file `tests/TinyTitanMemory/MemoryToolForgetTests.swift`, `@Suite(.serialized)`, running the built `.build/debug/tinytitan-memory` -- the idiom `tests/TinyTitanRepack/Core/Command/RepackCLITests.swift:99-125` already uses, with the executable path asserted to exist before the process is spawned so the test cannot pass by not running. The lock is taken in the test process with `open` + `flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)` on `<journal>.lock`, which conflicts with the child's attempt exactly as a server's would; `SweepStaleWorkspacesTests.lock(_:)` already relies on and states that property. Three tests: a held workspace is refused (exit 1, the refusal on stderr, no `forgot` on stdout, both the journal and the holder's `.lock` still on disk); a free workspace is still forgotten (exit 0, `forgot free-project`, journal gone); `--yes` is still checked before the lock probe, so an unconfirmed `forget` asks for confirmation rather than for a server to be stopped. Mutation probe -- `main.swift` restored from `ea0c4f1` and the suite re-run -- fails the refusal test with 5 issues, and the recorded output is the defect itself: `stdout: forgot held-project`, `stderr:` empty, plus `the held journal was deleted anyway` and `the holder's .lock was unlinked out from under its flock`. The other two pass on both trees, which is deliberate: they are counter-tests, so the first cannot be greened by making `forget` always fail. File restored and checksum-verified. Suite: 3 tests passed in 0.036 s. Gates: swift-format ok; swiftlint 0.65.1 --strict ok, after it caught `String(decoding:as:)` twice and the failable `String(bytes:encoding:)` the Repack suite uses went in; file-length ok (largest 496), func-length ok (14 baselined, 0 new), force-cast, unbounded-read, sendable, test-skip, arch-path ok, test-hollow ok at 1675 bodies, docs ok (83 documents, 17 gates). Sibling sweep: `MemoryService.swift:189-196` removes the same three files (journal, `.lock`, `.compacting`) and IS guarded -- `guard !Self.isLockHeld(at: url) else { continue }` -- with `theCapLeavesALockedWorkspaceAlone` pinning it, so `forget` was the last unfenced deletion of a live workspace in `sources/`. NOT covered, and deliberately unchanged: `forget` still leaves a `.compacting` temp where the cap removes one. It is a compaction scratch file (`Journal.swift:358`), neither `discover(in:)` nor `projectFiles(under:)` reads that suffix, and a same-named workspace's next compaction truncates it at its derived path -- litter, not data loss, and not this row's defect.

tasks.fix-summary: Three halves, one rule: a bound is honoured in the direction the flag means, or the run refuses. `positiveOption` (main.swift) now reads `--timeout`, `--limit`, `--concurrency`, `--width` and `--height`, and fails with `X needs a positive number, not Y` naming the flag and the value before any request goes out; it is generic over `LosslessStringConvertible & Comparable & ExpressibleByIntegerLiteral` so the Double timeout and the four Int counts share one message and one check. `--interval` deliberately still goes through `numberOption`: its floor is documented behaviour ("default 30 s, floored at 2 s") and `FleetScanner` clamps it, so `--interval 1` meaning 2 s is the contract, not a wrong answer. `promptAll`'s cap is now literal -- `if let limit { work = Array(work.prefix(max(0, limit))) }` -- so a library caller asking for zero sessions gets none and a negative one cannot reach the trap; `max(1, concurrency)` stays, and it is load-bearing: measured on this toolchain, `stride(from: 0, to: 4, by: 0)` is `Fatal error: Stride size must not be zero` and exit 133, so a zero batch size is a crash the CLI would otherwise hand to the library. `tooSmall` prints its message when the window cannot hold it (`width >= message.count ? fit(center(...)) : message`) and puts the message first when there is only one line, so the guard's remedy survives the size that triggered it; that is the one place this tree prints past the width it was handed, and the comment says so and why. `--help` now states the rule. The reachability that does exist is at the journal itself: a `record` for a scope whose task is not in RAM stops at that guard and drops the turn, and a turn whose session id the memory store never opened (`ContinuityStore.swift:410`, `sessionIDs[id]`, populated by `sessionInit`) has to be begun by the journal, where a refused `.session` write returns nil from `session(for:)` and the turn is gone. To make them separate paths rather than one scenario twice, `RefusingJournal` gained a record-kind selector — refusing everything cannot tell the three ways a turn is lost apart. The comment on `record` now names the mechanism the `try?` depends on (the engine records before it throws; `recordTurn` asks), because that invariant is what makes the swallow acceptable and it is exactly the thing a reader of `guard … else { return }` cannot see. tasks.fix-summary: `FileJournal` cuts the file back to its last complete line when it opens it for writing, before anything is appended. `dropDanglingTail` (new `sources/ContinuityCore/Persistence/FileJournal+Opening.swift`) `fstat`s the descriptor, scans backwards in 64 KiB chunks for the final newline and `ftruncate`s away the bytes after it: every complete record survives, and the first record after a crash lands on its own line. A file with no newline anywhere is one partial record and empties, which is what replay of it already returned, so nothing a reader would have kept is lost. The scan reads through the append descriptor, which is what keeps the bytes it decides on and the truncate that follows from being separated by another open, so `openForAppend` moved from `O_WRONLY` to `O_RDWR` -- owner-only 0600, created by this process, so the read permission the flag asks for is the one it holds. The initializer's failure path gained the `close(descriptor)` it was missing, because the new call can throw after the descriptor is open and a thrown initializer never runs `deinit` -- the lock and the file would have leaked.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/include/tinytitan_kernels.h:17-24 and :37-44 (the two entry-point docs that said the widths 'round alike'), sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/int8_affine_gemv.c:9-13 (the 'deliberately parallel' header) and :104-115 (the reduction comment above `(d0+d1)+(d2+d3)`, now :116)
tasks.title: The C kernels document a bitwise agreement between the 4-bit and 8-bit widths that they do not have, and no test measured the claim
tasks.category: documentation claim stronger than the code, in a file with zero ledger coverage -- the class this audit kept finding, now in the kernels rather than the Swift
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D convergence, on the first pass over `sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/`, which no earlier row had touched. The prompt was the one that found AUD-189 and AUD-190: read a comment that states a property and ask whether anything asserts it. `int8_affine_gemv.c` said the 4-bit kernel's single accumulator and this one's four 'reduce to the same value for the same inputs', and `tinytitan_kernels.h` said both widths 'round alike at group boundaries'. Reading `int4_affine_gemv.c` showed why that cannot be: every int4 lane chains all sixteen of its products into one `float32x4`, while int8 keeps four and combines them as `(d0+d1)+(d2+d3)`.
tasks.evidence-before: Three measurements, the first in the committed test and two by scratch C probes against the real kernels. (1) RED, the test asserting the claimed identity: `Expectation failed: four == eight` -- 4-bit `[955.4322, 955.4322, 955.4322]` against 8-bit `[955.43225, 955.43225, 955.43225]` for the same 256 products, scale BF16 1.0, bias 0.0, exit 1, 1 issue. (2) 400,000 randomized rows through both C entry points: 256,735 bitwise mismatches, 64.1838%, and the probe exits 1 on any mismatch. (3) 80,000 rows at the same scale, checked against a double-precision reference: 51,605 mismatches (64.51%), worst relative error 1.844e-03 for int4 and 2.570e-03 for int8; re-run with unit-scale `x` at 80,000 rows: 55,094 mismatches (68.87%), 1.060e-02 and 3.835e-03. So both widths are right to well under a percent of the row and differ in the last bits, exactly as the reduction orders predict. What nothing showed was a consumer of the stronger claim: no CPU golden target exists (`benchmark/golden/` is GPU greedy generation), the side-engine is validated against `tools/qwen35_reference.py` rather than against the other width, and no test compares a CPU row to a Metal row -- `docs/v4.4-decode-width-plan.md:552` already documents CPU/GPU agreement as 'to a rounding error', which is the same fact the kernels' own headers denied.
tasks.fix-summary: The three claims now say what is true: the two kernels share the *factoring* `scale * sum(q*x) + bias * sum(x)` per group, which is the contract, and the reduction inside a group is not shared, so reordering one kernel moves the last bits of its own width instead of breaking an exact agreement between the widths. No numerics changed -- the accumulators and their order are untouched, which is the rule in `AGENTS.md` (do not alter numerics unless asked). The test is replaced with the honest assertion: `bothWidthsAgreeToWithinARoundingErrorNotBitForBit` feeds identical products to both widths through `CPUOps.gemv`, the wrapper the engine itself calls, and bounds each row's gap by that row's own total absolute magnitude (`1e-6 * sum(|w|*|x|)`) rather than by the row's value, because a fp32 sum that cancels cannot bound its own roundings. `matchesTheFourBitReferenceOnRepresentableValues` is renamed from `agreesWithTheFourBitPathOnRepresentableValues` and re-documented: it dequantises at 4 bits in Swift and checks the 8-bit kernel against that oracle, so it never compared two kernels at all, and its old name plus doc ('it is why the two kernels factor the accumulation identically') read as if it did.
tasks.evidence-after: GREEN: `Test run with 7 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.196 seconds`. Mutation, so the new test is proved to be measuring the claim and not the ambient tolerance: `vzipq_u8(lo, hi)` -> `vzipq_u8(hi, lo)` in `int4_affine_gemv.c` (swapping which nibble is element 2k, i.e. changing the products the 4-bit kernel pairs) produced `row 0: gap 0.6291504 over 0.00095543225 (954.8031 vs 955.43225)` and the file was then restored -- `git diff --stat` on it empty. Full serial suite `swift test --no-parallel`, exit 0: 1712 tests in 253 suites across the 7 targets, 0 failures (`/tmp/suite191.log`) -- one test more than AUD-190's 1711/253, which is this one. `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH tools/lint.sh all`, exit 0 across all eighteen gates (`/tmp/lint191.log`); `test-hollow` now counts 1686 bodies, up from 1685, none hollow. Sibling sweep, in the order the sweep found them: (1) `int4_affine_gemv.c` re-read whole -- its header makes no cross-width claim at all (it is about why the C loop beats the Swift one, and about the mask/shift/zip unpack), so the only false statements were the two in the 8-bit file and the pair in the shared header, and nothing in the 4-bit kernel needed changing; (2) `tinytitan_kernels.h` scanned for every other equality-shaped phrase -- the remaining ones are about the affine *format* (one BF16 scale and one bias per 64 elements) and about element packing, both of which the tests do pin; (3) the `moe.metal` SIMD row (`moe_affine_gemv_row_simd`, :515-599) owns elements differently per lane (`e = g*64 + lane*2`) and reduces with `simd_sum`, so CPU-vs-GPU is the same story one level up -- **not filed**, because nothing claims bitwise identity there; the plan document already states the tolerance, and adding a CPU-to-Metal bitwise test would assert a property the design does not promise. Not verified, and recorded rather than glossed: no model was loaded, so `tools/golden-baseline.sh --check` and `LibraryContractTests` remain **not checked** for this change; they cannot be run against a CPU-only comment-and-test diff anyway, and neither was any kernel source modified. Residual: the 64-69% figure is measured on pseudorandom `x` at the widths' own toy geometry (256 columns), not on a shipping tensor -- the direction of the finding does not depend on it, but a future row that needs the rate should re-measure at real shapes.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitan/Infrastructure/ModelIO/ManifestReader.swift:145 (the peek's literal `maxBytes: 4 * 1024 * 1024`) against :20 (`defaultMaxBytes` = 64 MiB, which every other reader of the same file uses), and the two places the refusal is fatal: sources/TinyTitanLib/Engine.swift:66-70 and sources/TinyTitanLib/ServerModelSession+Loading.swift:98
tasks.title: `peekFamily`/`peekIdentity` read `manifest.json` with the 4 MiB ceiling the load moved off two years ago, so the front door refuses the installs the ceiling exists to admit
tasks.category: one bound declared twice, only one of them raised -- a supported model cannot be opened, and the error names the wrong thing
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D convergence, on a sweep for on-disk numbers reaching an allocation or a bound without a check between them (`SearchWorkspace` over the manifest/layout/receipt -> MTLBuffer/grid/loop-bound paths). That sweep came back mostly with guards already in place and named (`ResidentIndex.swift:91-124`'s payload-fit check, `PreadExpertStreamer.swift:189-218`'s overflow-checked range and `Int(exactly:)` stride, `PackedExpertsLayout.expert(layer:expert:)`'s bounds-checked indexing, `validateExecutableGeometry`'s tile and head ceilings), and it was the grep behind it -- every `maxBytes:` call site in `sources/` -- that showed one literal where every sibling names the constant.
tasks.evidence-before: RED on the unmodified tree, in a test that pads a toy manifest's `files` table the way a real per-tensor table grows: `Expectation failed: peekError == nil` -- `peekFamily refused a 14779152-byte manifest: Optional(resident index is corrupt: manifest.json size 14779152 exceeds metadata cap 4194304)` (`Test run with 34 tests in 2 suites failed after 0.535 seconds with 1 issue`, exit 1; 120,000 added entries the first time, 60,000 in the committed test). The mechanism is `SSDAIModelDirectory.readMetadata` refusing before it allocates (`:79-83`), which is the right behaviour with the wrong number: `ManifestReader.load`/`read` take `defaultMaxBytes` (64 MiB) and this one call site carried a bare `4 * 1024 * 1024`. Reachability is the front door, not a corner: `Engine.swift:66` calls `peekFamily` first and maps *any* error from it to `TinyTitanError.notAnInstall`, and `ServerModelSession+Loading.swift:98` propagates it before any manifest is read at the raised ceiling; `ModelCatalog.swift:235, :363`, `ModelRouter.swift:168`, `ModelSessionPlan.swift:173, :181` and `AffineSnapshot+Loading.swift:119` (the CPU side-engine) call the same function. So the class is not hypothetical either -- `ManifestReader.swift:10-19` and `runtimeAndRepackerAgreeOnTheManifestCeiling`'s own doc record the incident this ceiling was raised for: KAT-Coder-V2.5-Dev's manifest is 6.25 MB, it passed `--verify-install`, and the runtime refused to load it. The fix moved the runtime's ceiling to match the repacker's and asserted the two equal; the peek was left at 4 MiB, which is why the existing equality assertion could not see it -- it compares the named constants, and the offending value is a literal.
tasks.evidence-after: GREEN after the one-line change: `Test run with 34 tests in 2 suites passed after 0.403 seconds`, exit 0. The RED run above *is* the mutation evidence for this test -- the same tree three minutes earlier with the literal in place failed, and only `theFamilyPeekUsesTheManifestCeilingTheLoadUses` failed, so it is measuring the bound and not the fixture. Full serial suite `swift test --no-parallel` exit 0: 1714 tests in 253 suites across the 7 run groups (`/tmp/suite192.log`). `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 across the eighteen gates (`/tmp/lint192.log`). Sibling sweep, the two questions the fix raises: (1) is the bound declared anywhere else? No -- grepping every `maxBytes:` site in `sources/` gives `ManifestReader.defaultMaxBytes` at `Model+Loading.swift:54`, `ModelCatalog.swift:287`, `AffineSnapshot+Loading.swift:15`, `ANEPrefillAttention+Sidecar.swift:84`, `Detokenizer.swift:50`, `CPUCommands.swift:236`, `PLEConstants.defaultMaxBytes` defined *as* `ManifestReader.defaultMaxBytes`, `VerifiedInstallReceiptReader.defaultMaxBytes` and `PackedExpertsLayoutReader.defaultMaxBytes` for their own documents, and `SSDAIFormatV1.residentIndexMaxBytes`/`packedExpertsLayoutMaxBytes` (32 MiB / 128 MiB) for the index and the layout, each used through its constant; `:145` was the only literal left, and the guard now is that one name. (2) does the same divergence exist on the other side of the boundary? `plugins/dsh-tinytitan/src/catalog-scan.js` reads the manifest with `readFileSync` and no size cap (`:77`), so the plugin's scanner cannot refuse a large install -- checked because it documents itself as mirroring `peekIdentity`. What was NOT verified, and why: no KAT-Coder install exists on this host (`models/` holds the two Qwen3.8 installs only) and `AGENTS.md` forbids fetching one to satisfy a check, so the reproduction is a synthetic manifest that crosses the same boundary, and the 6.25 MB figure for the real file is the one already recorded in `ManifestReader.swift:10-19` rather than a fresh measurement. Its order of magnitude is not in doubt -- the file is a table with an entry per tensor whose width differs from the base, and KAT-Coder is the widest install here. No model was loaded, so `tools/golden-baseline.sh --check` and `LibraryContractTests` remain **not checked** for this change; the load path it touches is the one they would exercise, and the change is a ceiling, not a numerics change.
tasks.fix-summary: The peek reads the manifest with the same ceiling as the load: `maxBytes: Self.defaultMaxBytes` replaces the bare `4 * 1024 * 1024`, so there is one number for `manifest.json` in the runtime and `Engine`/`ServerModelSession` can reach the architecture of any install `--verify-install` accepts. No error-shape change: the refusal still comes from `readMetadata` for a file above 64 MiB, which is the bound that exists to stop an unbounded allocation before the decoder copies it.

tasks.fix-summary: RequestDecodingFailure.serverError(_:body:) (62 lines, new file) tells the two client bugs apart: a DecodingError whose bytes are not a JSON document at all (re-parsed with JSONSerialization .fragmentsAllowed, affordable because this only runs on a request already being refused) keeps invalid_json / "malformed JSON request"; everything else becomes invalid_value with the decoder's own codingPath rendered in the dotted form the validators already use (messages.0.content), and a non-DecodingError or an empty path gets the honest nameless wording under @unknown default.
